T272=27\left(\frac{T_2}{7}\right)^2 = 27
T2=7×27T_2 = 7 \times \sqrt{27}
T2=7×33T_2 = 7 \times 3\sqrt{3}

The approximate new time period is 36 hours.

which is positive for \(0<t<2\)

Differentiating logarithmically,

Thus \(F'(t)=0\) when \(n_1(2-t)=n_2t\)

Hence the unique stationary point is \(t=\dfrac{2n_1}{n_1+n_2}\)

and \(F\) has a local maximum there.

If \(n_2\) is even, \(f=F\),

so \(f\) has a local maximum in \((3,5)\)

If \(n_2\) is odd, \(f=-F\),

so \(f\) has a local minimum in \((3,5)\)

In option \(\mathrm{A}\),

\(n_2=4\) is even,

so a local maximum exists.

In option \(\mathrm{B}\),

\(n_2=3\) is odd,

so a local minimum exists.

In option \(\mathrm{C}\),

\(n_2=5\) is odd,

so the stationary point is a local minimum, not a local maximum.

In option \(\mathrm{D}\),

\(n_2=6\) is even,

so a local maximum exists

The distance of the origin from the centroid of the triangle whose two sides have the equations \( x-2 y+1=0 \) and \( 2 x-y-1=0 \) and whose orthocenter is \( \left(\frac{7}{3}, \frac{7}{3}\right) \) is:

The two given sides are \(x-2y+1=0\) and \(2x-y-1=0\).

Their point of intersection is one vertex, say \(A\).

From the first equation, \(x=2y-1\).

Substituting in the second equation, \(2(2y-1)-y-1=0\).

Thus \(3y-3=0\), so \(y=1\) and \(x=1\).

Hence \(A=(1,1)\).

The slope of \(x-2y+1=0\) is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Therefore, the altitude from the vertex on the second side has slope \(-2\).

It passes through the orthocenter \(H\left(\dfrac{7}{3},\dfrac{7}{3}\right)\).

Its equation is \(y-\dfrac{7}{3}=-2\left(x-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)\), or \(y=-2x+7\).

The second side is \(y=2x-1\).

Solving \(2x-1=-2x+7\), we get \(x=2\) and \(y=3\).

Hence one vertex is \(C=(2,3)\).

The slope of \(2x-y-1=0\) is \(2\).

Therefore, the other altitude has slope \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Through \(H\), its equation is \(y-\dfrac{7}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(x-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)\), or \(y=-\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{7}{2}\).

The first side is \(y=\dfrac{x+1}{2}\).

Solving \(\dfrac{x+1}{2}=-\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{7}{2}\), we get \(x=3\) and \(y=2\).

Hence the third vertex is \(B=(3,2)\).

The centroid is \(G=\left(\dfrac{1+3+2}{3},\dfrac{1+2+3}{3}\right)=(2,2)\).

Therefore, the distance of the centroid from the origin is \(OG=\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt{2}\).

Hence the correct option is \(C\).

questions.question:
Let f and g be twice differentiable even functions on \((-2,2)\) such that f14=0, f12 =0, f1=1 and g34=0, g1=2. Then the minimum number of solutions of fx g''x+f'xg'x=0 in \((-2,2)\) is equal to.

 

[JEE Main 2022, 29 June (Shift 2)]
questions.explanation:
Define \(h(x)=f(x)g'(x)\).

\(h'(x)=f'(x)g'(x)+f(x)g''(x)\).

Therefore, the given equation \(f(x)g''(x)+f'(x)g'(x)=0\) is 

\(h'(x)=0\).

Since \(f\) is even and \(f\left(\dfrac14\right)=0\),

we also have \(f\left(-\dfrac14\right)=0\).

Since \(f\) is even and \(f\left(\dfrac12\right)=0\),

we also have \(f\left(-\dfrac12\right)=0\).

Hence \(h\left(-\dfrac12\right)=h\left(-\dfrac14\right)=h\left(\dfrac14\right)=h\left(\dfrac12\right)=0\).

Also, \(g\) is even and differentiable.

The derivative of an even differentiable function is odd,

so \(g'(0)=0\).

Therefore, \(h(0)=f(0)g'(0)=0\).

Thus \(h\) has five distinct zeros at \(-\dfrac12,-\dfrac14,0,\dfrac14,\dfrac12\).

By Rolle's theorem,

\(h'\) has at least one zero in each interval between two consecutive zeros of \(h\).

These intervals are \(\left(-\dfrac12,-\dfrac14\right)\), \(\left(-\dfrac14,0\right)\), \(\left(0,\dfrac14\right)\), and \(\left(\dfrac14,\dfrac12\right)\).

Therefore, \(h'(x)=0\) has at least four solutions in \((-2,2)\).

To claim that four is the minimum,

it is enough to provide one example with exactly four solutions.

Take \(f(x)=\dfrac{64}{45}\left(x^2-\dfrac1{16}\right)\left(x^2-\dfrac14\right)\).

This function is even, and direct substitution gives

\(f\left(\dfrac14\right)=0\), \(f\left(\dfrac12\right)=0\), and \(f(1)=1\).

Take \(g(x)=\dfrac{32}{7}x^2-\dfrac{18}{7}\).

This function is even, and direct substitution gives

\(g\left(\dfrac34\right)=0\) and \(g(1)=2\).

For these functions, \(h'(x)\) is a non-zero constant multiple of

\(5x^4-\dfrac{15}{16}x^2+\dfrac1{64}\).

Put \(u=x^2\).

 \(5u^2-\dfrac{15}{16}u+\dfrac1{64}=0\).

Its discriminant is \(\left(\dfrac{15}{16}\right)^2-4(5)\left(\dfrac1{64}\right)=\dfrac{225}{256}-\dfrac{80}{256}=\dfrac{145}{256}>0\).

The sum of the roots is \(\dfrac{15}{80}>0\),

and their product is \(\dfrac1{320}>0\).

Therefore, both roots in \(u\) are positive and distinct.

Each positive root of \(u=x^2\) gives two real values of \(x\),

so there are exactly four real solutions.

Hence the minimum number of solutions is \(4\).
